q: Describe the relationship between summer temperature and spruce killed.
Hotter summers, more spruce killed, with a sharp increase above about 16 °C (40 at 15.1 °C, 600 at 17.2 °C).
Explain the 2018 peak, using two factors from the table.
2018 was the hottest year, so beetles develop faster and can fit two generations into one summer. It was also the driest, so drought-stressed trees make less resin and cannot fight off the beetles.
2020 was cooler than 2018, but damage stayed high. Suggest why.
The huge beetle population from 2018–2019 carried over, and many trees were still weakened.
Explain why it is hard to separate the effects of temperature and rainfall in these data.
Hot summers were also dry: the two variables are correlated, so either could be the cause.
Suggest one way forest managers could reduce the damage.
Remove infested trees quickly, or plant mixed forests instead of spruce alone.

21.t: Working with data: caterpillars and chicks
q: Calculate the mismatch (hatching day minus caterpillar peak) in 1970 and in 2020.
1970: 148 − 150 = -2 days (chicks just before the peak). 2020: 139 − 132 = +7 days (chicks a week late).
Calculate how many days per decade each peak has moved earlier.
Caterpillars 18 days in 5 decades = 3.6 days per decade. Birds 9 days = 1.8 days per decade.
Explain why the caterpillar peak has moved earlier.
Warmer springs: oak leaves open earlier and caterpillar development is driven by temperature.
Suggest why the birds have advanced less than the caterpillars.
Laying is timed partly by day length, which has not changed, and birds must lay weeks before the caterpillars appear.
Use the fledging data to evaluate the effect of the mismatch on great tits.
Chicks fledged fell by about a quarter (8.2 to 6.1), fitting less food when chicks need it most; but other causes (predators, weather) could also contribute.
